title: Tenses: reported speech, conditionals and wishes

rule.body: After a past reporting verb, tenses usually move back (is to was, will to would). Conditionals: If + present, will + verb; If + past, would + verb; If + had + past participle, would have + past participle. Use 'were' for all persons in unreal situations and after 'wish'. After 'It is high time', use the past tense. In future time clauses after 'when', 'until' or 'as soon as', use the present tense, not 'will'.
rule.example: If I were you, I would apologise before he leaves.

questions.stem: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the match.
questions.explanation: This is a real future possibility, so it is a first conditional: If + present, will + verb.

questions.stem: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation: I am not you, so this is unreal. With 'would' in the result, the if-clause takes 'were'.

questions.stem: I will call you when I ___ home.
questions.explanation: In a future time clause after 'when', we use the present tense, not 'will'.
A wish about the present uses a past form, and 'were' is used for all persons after 'wish'.

questions.stem: When I met Bola last week, he said that he ___ to Abuja the next day.
questions.explanation: The reporting verb 'said' is past and 'the next day' is already past, so the tense moves back to 'was travelling'.

questions.stem: If he had studied harder, he ___ the examination.
questions.explanation: 'Had studied' shows a third conditional about the past, so the result is 'would have passed'.

questions.stem: It is high time you ___ to bed.
questions.explanation: After 'It is high time', we use the past tense even though we mean now, so 'went' is correct.

questions.stem: The teacher asked us whether we ___ our homework the night before.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after 'asked', a past action ('the night before') moves back to the past perfect: 'had done'.

questions.stem: I wish I ___ the answer yesterday.
questions.explanation: A wish about the past ('yesterday') uses the past perfect: 'had known'.

questions.stem: We will not start the meeting until the chairman ___.
questions.explanation: 'Until' begins a future time clause here, so it takes the present tense 'arrives', not 'will arrive'.
